The instrument lists look alike — both have gong circles, both have a melodic percussion instrument (the xylophone in Thailand, the pitched drum circle in Myanmar), both have a four-reed shawm, both have drums — but the organising logic is exactly opposite. The Myanmar drummer is the leader, and the drums are pitched and can play melody; the Thai drum only keeps time, the melody goes to the xylophone and the pi, and the drum takes no part in the melody. So a Myanmar ensemble sounds like the drums are talking, and a Thai ensemble sounds like the xylophone is talking.

That makes the transmission of the Thai classical repertoire firmer than many Southeast Asian traditions, but what got standardised is the structural melody, not the ornament: players are still expected to add ornaments to the structure, only those ornaments have to sit inside the shared frame. The reason piphat recordings today differ so little from one another has to do with this teaching system.
